segments.say: Before you sleep, picture yourself looking once more towards the bedroom window. The curtains are drawn, but there's a thin gap between them, and through it you can see a narrow strip of the night outside. The garden, white with frost. The dark shape of a tree. And the sky, deep blue and full of stars.

And then, as you watch, something changes, very softly. A single white flake drifts past the gap in the curtains. Then another. Then a few more, slowly, turning in the air. It's beginning to snow. Not a storm, nothing like that. Just a gentle, quiet snowfall, the kind that comes on very still nights.

Picture the snowflakes falling past the window, slowly, slowly, each one taking its time. Some drift straight down. Some wander a little to the side and then carry on. None of them are in a hurry. They float down through the dark, catching a little light from somewhere, and disappear below the windowsill, into the garden.

Picture the garden below, slowly turning whiter and softer as the snow settles. The path disappears under a smooth white blanket. The flowerpots on the step grow little white caps. The bare branches of the tree gather thin white lines along their tops. Everything becomes rounder, and softer, and quieter, under the falling snow.

Snow has a sound of its own, or rather, an absence of sound. As it falls, the world grows quieter and quieter. The snow softens every edge, muffles every footstep, hushes every far-off road. Listen to that hush now. A deep, soft, peaceful quiet, spreading out over the whole sleeping town, house by house, street by street.

The garden through the gap in the curtains, slowly filling with snow. There's nothing to do but watch, or not watch at all. The snow will keep falling, softly and steadily, whether you're looking or not.

Imagine the snow falling over everywhere you walked tonight. Over the little church hall, settling on its roof. Over the frosty street and the cat's garden wall. Over the high street and its sleeping windows. Over the square and the café and the old memorial. Over the river, melting softly into the dark water. Over the green bridge and the oak and the bench.

Picture your own footprints from tonight, all the way from the hall to your front door, slowly filling with snow, one by one, until they've disappeared completely. The whole evening, smoothed over and made new. By morning, the town will be white and fresh and still, as if the day had been gently wiped clean.

That's what sleep can do, too. It can soften the edges of the day, and cover over the little worries, and smooth everything out, so that you wake up fresh. You don't have to carry anything from today into tomorrow. Let the snow cover it all, softly, and let it rest.

And while the snow falls outside, you're warm inside, tucked up under your covers. There's something deeply comforting in that, being warm and safe in bed while the cold, quiet world goes white outside the window. Let yourself feel it. The warmth all around you. The softness. The safety.

You might let each snowflake be a breath. As one drifts down past the window, breathe in, slowly. As it disappears below the sill, breathe out, slowly. Then the next one. In. And out. Each flake slower than the last. Each breath softer and deeper, carrying you a little further down, towards sleep.

Now picture the gap in the curtains slowly closing, as if someone had drawn them together very gently. The strip of snowy night grows narrower, and narrower, and then it's gone. There's only the soft dark of the room now, and the faint, faint hush of the snow outside, falling and falling, all night long.

Let yourself sink deeper into that soft dark. Deeper into the bed. Deeper into the quiet. Your body heavy and warm. Your breathing slow and easy. Your mind soft and far away, drifting like a snowflake, down, and down, and down, until it settles gently somewhere peaceful and still.
